title: Cauchy-Euler
body:
Differential equations of the form
$$
ax^2y''(x)+bxy'(x)+y(x)=f(x)
$$
Can be solved by deriving a characteristic equation
$$
ar^2+(b-a)r+c=0
$$
And introducing the substitution
$$
x=e^t\iff x=\ln(t)
$$
Then solving using [[Undetermined Coefficients]]

> [!warning] Two transcription slips in the lines above, left in place rather than overwritten
> - The equation should read $ax^2y'' + bxy' + \mathbf{c}y = f(x)$. As written the $y$ term has
>   coefficient $1$, but the characteristic equation below it uses $c$, so the two lines do not
>   match.
> - The substitution should read $x = e^t \iff t = \ln(x)$. As written both sides define $x$.

---

The point of the equation: the coefficient of each derivative carries exactly as many powers of $x$
as the order of that derivative, so $x^ky^{(k)}$ is scale invariant and the whole equation is
unchanged by stretching $x$. That is why it solves in closed form despite having variable
coefficients, and it is the only such family in the course.

The substitution $x = e^t$ turns it into a constant-coefficient equation in $t$, at which point it
is a [[Homogeneous ODE]] (or a [[Non-Homogeneous ODE]] if $f \neq 0$) and the characteristic
equation above is what you get. Equivalently, guess $y = x^r$ directly and read off the same
polynomial. The three root cases carry over unchanged, with $x^r$ in place of $e^{rt}$:

| Roots | Solution |
|---|---|
| Real, distinct | $c_1x^{r_1} + c_2x^{r_2}$ |
| Repeated $r$ | $c_1x^r + c_2x^r\ln x$ |
| Complex $\alpha\pm\beta i$ | $x^\alpha(c_1\cos(\beta\ln x) + c_2\sin(\beta\ln x))$ |

The $\ln x$ is what $t$ becomes under the substitution, which is why the repeated-root case picks
up a logarithm here and a factor of $t$ there.

**$x = 0$ is a regular singular point** of this equation, which is the reason it is the worked
example in every treatment of [[Series Solutions]]: the Frobenius indicial equation for a general
equation is the Cauchy-Euler characteristic equation of its leading behaviour.
